1.goal: To open on something she has actually wanted to ask and did not, and to say once where the hour ends.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class and whether she wrote the six questions.
Say what today is: she asks six questions now, before anything is explained, and at the end of the hour she finds out three things about you.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “You ask me six questions now. Nothing gets corrected. At the end of the hour you will look at them again — and you will find out three things about me.”
1.expected: Something she wanted to ask a teacher, a video, a person online. It may come in Portuguese.
1.support: Offer two: something at school, or something outside it.
1.challenge: Ask what stopped her from asking it.
1.monitoring: Whether the thing that stopped her was the words or the order.
1.evidence: What she says stops her asking. It is worth more than any of the six questions.
1.transition: Move on as soon as she knows nothing is being corrected in the next ten minutes.

2.goal: To collect six questions of hers, unhelped, as the evidence the whole lesson is measured against.
2.interaction: S–T. She asks, you answer briefly.
run: Ask for the six, in the three pairs on screen: weekend, work, anything.
Write each one down word for word, mistakes and all. Do not correct, do not react to the form.
Answer each question briefly and honestly, so that asking feels like it produced something.
If she asks whether a question was right, say you are writing them down and that you will look at them together at the end.
exact: Setting it up: “Six questions about my week. Nothing here is corrected — I am just writing them down.”
If she asks whether it was right: “I am writing it down. We look at all six at the end of the hour.”
2.expected: Six questions, some of them with the order scrambled. Her profile says the problem is occasional, so several will be perfectly formed.
2.support: If she cannot think of one, give her the topic and not the words: “Something about Sunday.”
2.challenge: Ask for a seventh that she would not normally dare to ask.
2.monitoring: Which ones come out scrambled and of what kind: missing auxiliary, double past, or no inversion at all.
2.evidence: The six questions, verbatim. This is the diagnostic of the lesson and the record that matters most.
2.transition: Move on once you have six written down.

3.goal: To meet six real questions in a context where nobody is thinking about grammar.
3.interaction: T–S, reading the exchange out loud together.
run: Read the exchange out loud with her, taking one side each.
Find the six questions together and underline them, without discussing any of them.
Ask which one she would find hardest to say, and why.
3.expected: Six questions found. The one she names as hardest is usually the one with did.
3.support: If she cannot find all six, tell her how many are in each half.
3.challenge: Ask which question in the exchange gets the most useful answer.
3.monitoring: Whether she notices anything about the form on her own. Some students do, here.
3.evidence: Which question she calls the hardest. It usually predicts what went wrong on screen 2.
3.transition: Move on when the six are underlined.

4.goal: To sort real questions from ones that only look like questions, before any rule exists.
run: Let her mark the three on her own.
Check them one at a time, and on each wrong one ask the same question: what is missing, or what did not move?
Do not state the rule. Screen 6 does that, and only after screen 5.
exact: On each wrong one: “What would have to move for this to be a question?”
4.expected: The three correct ones. Which subjects you chose? is the one most often accepted, because it is perfectly understandable.
4.support: Read the statement version out loud right before the question version, and ask what is different.
4.challenge: Ask her to fix the three wrong ones out loud.
4.monitoring: Whether she can hear the difference before she can name it.
4.evidence: Whether she accepted the two that changed nothing. Those are the same shape as her own errors.
4.transition: Move on when the three are marked and the wrong ones have been discussed.

5.goal: To locate the auxiliary in each sentence and see that its position is the whole difference.
run: Let her place the six.
Check them by reading each pair out loud back to back: the statement, then the question.
Leave the last one alone for now — it is the exception, and screen 7 is about it.
5.expected: Four in front, two behind, one with no auxiliary at all. Who sits over there is the odd one out.
5.support: Ask her to point at the little word with her finger before she chooses.
5.challenge: Ask her to turn one of the two statements into a question out loud.
5.monitoring: Whether she finds the pattern herself. If she says it out loud before screen 6, the discovery worked.
5.evidence: Whether she named the pattern before being shown it.
5.transition: Move on when the six are placed. If she has already said the rule, tell her so on the next screen.

6.goal: To state the rule in one line, after she has already seen it, and to name the second thing that changes with did.
run: Read the three pairs on screen out loud.
Ask the question on the screen: in the third pair, what changed besides the new word?
Open the reveal only after she has answered, and read it with her.
If she named the pattern on the screen before, say that this is her rule, not the screen's.
exact: If she does not see the second change: “Look at the verb. It was ‘chose’. What is it now?”
6.expected: The auxiliary moves in front of the subject; where there is none, do / does / did comes in; and the main verb goes back to its plain form.
6.support: Cover the third pair and do the first two only, then uncover it.
6.challenge: Ask her to explain the rule back to you in one sentence, in her own words.
6.monitoring: Whether the double past is new information or something she already avoided.
6.evidence: Her own formulation of the rule. Write it down if it is good — it is worth more than the screen's.
6.transition: Move on once the reveal has been read.

7.goal: To handle the one case where nothing moves, by asking who is doing the action.
run: Read the two lines on screen and ask the question: why has the first one no do in it?
Let her do the six items, then check them.
Give her one test to keep: is the question word the one doing the action?
exact: The test, said once and repeated: “Ask yourself: who is doing it? If it is the question word, nothing moves.”
7.expected: Three with no auxiliary, three with one. The pairs are built so the only difference is who acts.
7.support: On each item, ask who did the action, and answer it together before she chooses.
7.challenge: Ask her to make one more pair of her own, one of each kind.
7.monitoring: Whether she uses the test or guesses.
7.evidence: Whether the exception sticks or collapses back into the rule.
7.transition: Move on once the six are done and the test has been said out loud.

8.goal: To rebuild six questions quickly, saying each one out loud before checking it.
8.interaction: S alone, at speed, with you timing loosely.
run: Say the rule of the game: choose, say it out loud, then check. In that order.
Let her go through the six without stopping. Do not comment between items.
At the end, go back only to the ones that were wrong, and ask what moved.
exact: The rule of the game: “Choose, say it out loud, then check. Saying it is the part that makes it stick.”
8.expected: Five or six right. Who taught you English? is the one that catches people, because it is the exception in the middle of a drill about the rule.
8.support: If she is choosing without saying, stop and ask her to say the last one out loud before moving on.
8.challenge: Ask her to say all six again from memory, in order.
8.monitoring: Speed and accuracy together. Getting it right slowly is not the same as having it.
8.evidence: How many were right at speed, and whether she actually said them out loud.
8.transition: Move on when the six are done.

9.goal: To hand her back her own six questions from the start of the hour and let her hear the difference.
9.interaction: T–S. You read hers; she says them again.
run: Read her first question back exactly as she said it.
Ask her to say it the way she would say it now. Take her version without comment.
Do all six, quickly. Where one was already right the first time, say so and move on.
Count out loud at the end how many she changed herself.
exact: Reading one back: “You asked me: ‘…’. How would you say it now?”
On the one that was already right: “That one was right the first time. You had it before we started.”
9.expected: She corrects most of them without help. That is the point of the screen, and it is the evidence the lesson worked.
9.support: If she cannot see what to change, ask where the little word is.
9.challenge: Ask her to say which of the six she would still not be sure about tomorrow.
9.monitoring: How many she fixes with no help at all.
9.evidence: Screen 9 against screen 2, in numbers. It is the clearest measure this lesson produces.
9.transition: Move on when the six have been said again.

10.goal: To write three real questions she would like to ask you and has never asked.
10.interaction: S alone, writing. You stay out of it.
run: Give her five minutes and quiet. Writing before speaking is how she produces her best sentences.
Do not look at what she is writing and do not correct it.
Say once, before she starts, that she will not be allowed to read them on the next screen.
exact: Before she starts: “Write three. On the next screen you turn the paper over — so write things you will remember.”
10.expected: Three real questions. If they are safe and general, the next screen will be flat, so it is worth saying that out loud.
10.support: Offer two areas she has not asked about: something before you were a teacher, something outside work.
10.challenge: Ask for one she thinks you might not want to answer.
10.monitoring: Whether the written questions are better formed than the spoken ones. The gap is worth knowing.
10.evidence: The three written questions, and how they compare with the six spoken ones.
10.transition: Move on when three are written.

11.goal: To find out three things about you, by asking, with the paper turned over.
run: Ask her to turn the paper over before she asks the first one.
Answer every question briefly. A short answer is what leaves room for the second one.
Do not offer anything she did not ask for. If she moves on without following up, let her, and note it.
At the end, ask her to tell you the three things she found out.
exact: Setting it up: “Turn the paper over. Find out three things about me that you did not know an hour ago.”
If she moves on after one answer: “Is that all you want to know about that?”
11.expected: Three questions and at least two follow-ups built on your answers. The follow-up is the thing this screen exists for.
11.support: If she cannot remember her question, give her the first word only.
11.challenge: Answer one question with something surprising and say nothing more, so the follow-up has to come.
11.monitoring: How many questions came out of your answers rather than out of her list. Note the word order too, but do not act on it.
11.evidence: Number of follow-up questions, and whether she could ask without the paper. This is the main record of the lesson.
11.transition: Move on when she has told you the three things she found out.

12.goal: To close with the comparison, not with a correction.
run: Write one thing that worked and one thing to build on.
Put one of her questions from screen 2 and her own corrected version side by side in the boxes.
Open the replay and go through the six from the start of the hour: how many would she write differently now?
exact: Closing the comparison: “An hour ago you asked me these six. You have just fixed most of them yourself.”
12.expected: She recognizes most of her own changes. The ones she still cannot see are what the next block watches.
12.support: If she cannot see a change on one, leave it. It goes into the record, not into a longer explanation.
12.challenge: Ask which one she thinks she will get wrong again next week.
12.monitoring: Whether her sense of what she fixed matches what actually changed.
12.evidence: Which of the six she still cannot see. That is what carries into the next block.

13.goal: To close the lesson with what was worked on and where it goes.
13.interaction: T–S, ticking the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap and tick what was done.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Say the homework out loud: this week, ask one more question about the answer, instead of moving on.
exact: The homework: “This week, when someone answers you, ask one more thing about the answer. One. That is all.”
13.expected: Her own reading of the hour. The question about which answer was most interesting usually gets a real answer.
13.support: If the confidence is low, remind her how many of the six she corrected herself.
13.challenge: Ask which of the three things she found out surprised her.
13.monitoring: Whether she leaves thinking of questions as something she can do rather than something she gets wrong.
13.evidence: Her confidence marks, and what she said about the pre-class.
13.transition: End here. The next lesson is the one that closes the block: two minutes about her, and what she wants to do.
